passages.t: Wisdom handed down from a grandfather
passages.happening:
‘Listen, my sons, to a father’s instruction; pay attention and gain understanding’ (verse 1). The father tells his children that he was once a son himself, ‘tender and the only child of my mother’ (verse 3), and that his own father taught him.

Then he passes on his father's words: “Let your heart lay hold of my words; keep my commands and you will live” (verse 4). “Get wisdom, get understanding; do not forget my words or turn from them” (verse 5). “Wisdom is supreme; so acquire wisdom. And whatever you may acquire, gain understanding” (verse 7).

Wisdom is pictured like someone to be loved and held: ‘love her, and she will guard you’ (verse 6). ‘Prize her, and she will exalt you; if you embrace her, she will honor you’ (verse 8). She will crown the one who loves her (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Here are three generations: a grandfather, a father and his children. Wisdom is handed down. In the ancient world teaching was passed on by word of mouth in families and among scribes, and a teaching carried weight partly because of how old it was and who had passed it on.

Because the book is linked with Solomon, some readers hear this as Solomon remembering David and his mother Bathsheba, and the Bible does record David's charges to Solomon (1 Kings 2; 1 Chronicles 22 and 28). The chapter does not name them, though. The phrase ‘only child’ probably means beloved or unique, since Bathsheba had other sons (1 Chronicles 3:5). It may simply be the voice of every teaching father, remembering how he was taught.

Get is the Hebrew word qanah, the ordinary word for buying goods or property. It comes four times here. Verse 7 pushes it hard: whatever else you buy, buy understanding. Wisdom is worth spending everything on, the way a merchant would pay any price for a treasure.
passages.later: Moses told Israel to do exactly this: ‘Teach them to your children and grandchildren’ (Deuteronomy 4:9). And David charged Solomon: ‘As for you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve Him wholeheartedly and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches every heart’ (1 Chronicles 28:9).
passages.asks: Someone taught this father, and he teaches his children. Ask who passed on to you what you know of God, and give thanks for them. And ask who is listening to you now, and what you are handing on to them.

passages.happening:
‘Listen, my son, and receive my words, and the years of your life will be many’ (verse 10). The father will lead his son on straight paths, where he can walk and even run without stumbling (verses 11-12). ‘Hold on to instruction; do not let go. Guard it, for it is your life’ (verse 13).

‘Do not set foot on the path of the wicked or walk in the way of evildoers’ (verse 14). ‘Avoid it; do not travel on it. Turn from it and pass on by’ (verse 15). The wicked cannot even sleep until they have done harm, ‘For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence’ (verse 17).

Then a great contrast: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday. But the way of the wicked is like the darkest gloom; they do not know what makes them stumble” (verses 18-19).
passages.hearers:
Paths and roads were real things to the first hearers. Travel was on foot along rough tracks, where stones, ruts and holes could trip a traveler, and darkness made a road truly dangerous. The father's picture would be easy to feel.

Notice how firm the warning is. Do not set foot on the path, avoid it, do not travel on it, turn from it, pass on by. It is easier to stay off a road than to get off it once you are walking.

The wicked live on what they take from others, the way other people live on daily bread and wine. Their life is built on harm.

And the two paths move in opposite directions. The righteous walk into growing light, like the sun rising toward noon. The wicked walk into deeper darkness, and they do not even see what trips them.
passages.later: The first psalm ends with the same two ways: ‘For the LORD guards the path of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish’ (Psalm 1:6).
passages.asks: The father says to turn from the wrong road before you set foot on it. Ask whether there is a path you are standing at the edge of, and what it would mean to pass on by. And ask which way your own road is heading, toward more light or toward more darkness.

passages.happening:
‘My son, pay attention to my words; incline your ear to my sayings’ (verse 20). Keep them in your heart, ‘For they are life to those who find them, and health to the whole body’ (verse 22).

Then the father moves through the whole person. The heart: “Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life” (verse 23). The mouth: ‘Put away deception from your mouth; keep your lips from perverse speech’ (verse 24). The eyes: ‘Let your eyes look forward; fix your gaze straight ahead’ (verse 25). The feet: ‘Make a level path for your feet, and all your ways will be sure’ (verse 26). ‘Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your feet away from evil’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
In Hebrew thought the heart, lev, was not mainly the place of feelings, as it is in English. It was the center of the inner person: where a person thinks, decides, remembers and desires. Mind and will together. So guarding the heart means guarding the whole inner direction of a life, where choices, words and actions come from.

Springs mattered in a dry land. A town could only be built where there was a reliable spring. Life flows out of the heart the way water flows from a spring.

Guard is natsar, the word for a watchman keeping a city or a vineyard. In verse 6 wisdom guards the one who loves her. Here the son guards his own heart.

The father checks his son from the inside out: heart, mouth, eyes, feet. A level path was one cleared and smoothed, so a traveler would not trip. What a person is on the inside decides where he goes on the outside.
passages.later: Moses used the same words for keeping God's law: ‘you are not to turn aside to the right or to the left’ (Deuteronomy 5:32). And Hebrews echoes verse 26 when it tells tired believers, ‘Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed’ (Hebrews 12:13).
passages.asks: Everything flows from the heart. Ask what you let into your heart most days, and what is flowing out of it in your words. And ask where your eyes keep wandering, and what it would mean to fix your gaze straight ahead.
